h.strategy: Most obvious hypotheses follow a local story: an option matters more when its substitute is missing. These are usually rated likely and often fail. Instead, base hypotheses on robust statistical regularities. (1) Headroom: helpful edits help less in parents that are already strong, for example parents that already contain the strongest option elsewhere. (2) Harmful edits hurt more in strong parents and look harmless in weak parents, because of floor effects. (3) Saturation: adding a second copy of a strong option gives smaller gains than adding the first. (4) Removing an option costs less when the parent has several similar options. Choose conditions that many parents satisfy, so the effect is detectable. Cover several edited fields and both directions. In each 'why', state the obvious prediction and the reason the opposite should hold.

hyps.why: Obvious: removal hurts more in strong parents; but a redundant strong conv on edge 4 compensates, so removing edge 5 costs less.
Dropping a skip on the internal edge costs little compared with dropping a conv, since skip contributes little capacity.
A direct skip into the output helps weak parents; parents with a strong conv into node 3 have less headroom for it.
Skip's gain is largest in weak parents, so a strong conv on edge 5 shrinks it.
Parents with a strong output-side conv have less headroom, so extra conv1x1 on the internal edge adds less.
The internal conv3x3 gain shrinks when the cell already has conv3x3 on edge 4.
Saturation: a second skip path adds little over an existing direct skip to the output.
A skip already provides the gradient shortcut, so another skip into node 3 is redundant.
Floor effect: in an already crippled parent, removing another edge changes little, so the loss is smaller.
Obvious: removal always hurts; but when edge 3 is already none the cell is weak and near the floor, so the extra loss is smaller.
